# Results {#sec-results}

## Question-Level Harmonization Rates

Collapsing from pair-level to question-level — does each source question have at least one ACS question it can harmonize with? — produces the central finding:

<!-- TODO: Insert consolidation_rates.png figure -->

| Survey | Total Questions | F1 (Direct) | F2 (Conditional) | F3 (Not Feasible) | Harmonizable | Rate |
|--------|---------------:|------------:|-----------------:|-------------------:|-------------:|-----:|
| CPS | 240 | 37 (15.4%) | 65 (27.1%) | 138 (57.5%) | 102 | 42.5% |
| FoodAPS | 140 | 23 (16.4%) | 45 (32.1%) | 72 (51.4%) | 68 | 48.6% |

<!-- ✅ RECONCILED 2026-02-14: stage4_survey_summary.json confirms 102/42.5%. Stale exec summary said 100/41.7%. -->

Approximately **45% of source questions** have at least one viable harmonization path to ACS. The rates are remarkably stable across the two survey pairs despite their different purposes — CPS is a broad labor force survey, FoodAPS is a specialized food acquisition survey. This stability suggests the result reflects a structural property of the survey ecosystem, not a survey-specific artifact.

### Interpreting the Tiers

- **F1 questions (~16%)** are high-quality bridge variables. The source and ACS questions measure the same construct with compatible response formats. Cross-survey linkage requires only simple recoding.
- **F2 questions (~29%)** are usable bridge variables requiring documented statistical adjustment — typically temporal alignment or scale transformation. The underlying construct is the same; the measurement approach differs in addressable ways.
- **F3 questions (~55%)** have characterized barriers that prevent harmonization. The barrier diagnosis explains specifically *why* — information that is itself valuable for survey design.

### Pair-Level vs. Question-Level Rates

| Survey | Pair-Level Rate | Question-Level Rate |
|--------|:-:|:-:|
| CPS | 19.5% | 42.5% |
| FoodAPS | 20.6% | 48.6% |

The pair-level rates are much lower because each question is paired with many unrelated ACS questions (the combinatorial design). The question-level rate — "does this question have *any* viable match?" — is the operationally meaningful metric.

## Barrier Analysis

Among questions rated not harmonizable (F3), what prevents harmonization?

<!-- TODO: Insert barrier_distribution.png figure -->

| Barrier | CPS | FoodAPS |
|---------|:---:|:-------:|
| CC (Construct/Concept) | 85.1% | 88.9% |
| TC (Temporal) | 7.9% | 5.5% |
| RS (Response Scale) | 4.1% | 3.3% |
| PC (Population) | 0.7% | 0.9% |
| MC (Mode/Context) | 1.0% | 0.7% |
| PM (Precision) | 0.2% | 0.2% |

Construct mismatch dominates at ~87%. This is expected and, in an important sense, *desirable*: most question pairs that can't harmonize are measuring fundamentally different things. The surveys are specialized for a reason.

The actionable insight is in the remaining ~13%. Questions blocked by temporal mismatches, response scale differences, or population coverage gaps represent potentially addressable barriers — cases where survey redesign or statistical methods could unlock additional harmonization.

## Expert Review Triage

Not all questions receive a confident automated verdict. The triage system routes uncertain cases to expert review:

<!-- TODO: Insert expert_review_load.png figure -->

- **~76% auto-processed** with high confidence — no expert input needed
- **~24% (93 questions)** routed to expert review — uncertain or contested ratings

This division of labor is the design intent: AI handles the breadth (1,598 pairs across thousands of questions), while human experts focus their limited time on the genuinely ambiguous cases where judgment matters most.
